deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no derivation, formula or computation. It is a set of prose drafts, almost certainly preliminary formulations for Riemann's 1851 doctoral dissertation, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. Matches are cited from memory and are not verified against the printed text. Two separate passages appear.

(1) Boundary values (lines 1-5). This is a remark on the data of the boundary-value problem the dissertation solves through the Dirichlet-principle argument (Art. 16-19). The prescribed values of the real part, or of the auxiliary function g, along the boundary of the surface T need only satisfy one condition: they must not be discontinuous along a whole part (arc) of the boundary. Isolated discontinuities are therefore allowed. Any further restriction, such as continuity everywhere, is imposed only 'to avoid unnecessary complications here'.

This fits the next page (21r/22). There Riemann justifies the restriction by showing that the Dirichlet integral L = ∬ ((∂λ/∂x)^2 + (∂λ/∂y)^2) dT has the following property:
- If g is discontinuous along a line, then any λ that agrees with g outside a neighbourhood T' gives an L exceeding every bound C once T' is small enough.
- So a minimizer cannot track a jump along a curve.
- Isolated point discontinuities, by contrast, can be tolerated.

In modern terms: H^1 functions cannot have jump discontinuities along a curve, since their traces lie in H^{1/2}. Single points, however, have zero capacity in 2D.

(2) A definition of the 'simplicity' of a dependence law (Abhängigkeitsgesetz). A dependence (function) counts as simpler the fewer 'Grössenoperationen' are needed to determine it. Riemann lists these operations explicitly:
- addition and subtraction;
- multiplication and division;
- integration and differentiation.
He then glosses them as 'computational operations in which the commensurability of the quantities does not come into question'. That is, operations that do not depend on arithmetic or number-theoretic properties of the values, such as rationality. This belongs to the programmatic closing considerations of the dissertation (Art. 20): Riemann's method characterizes a function by its discontinuities and boundary conditions, independently of any expression by operations. He contrasts this with the classical notion of a function given by a formula.

Nothing here requires mathematical reconstruction beyond these restatements.
errors: No mathematical errors; there are no computations on the page. The claim that discontinuity along a boundary arc is the only essential restriction is consistent with the H^1/Dirichlet-energy argument on the next page. The Dirichlet-principle framework itself was later criticized by Weierstrass (1870) for assuming that the minimum is attained. That criticism concerns the method, not this page.

results.what: Boundary data for the Dirichlet-type problem need only avoid discontinuity along a whole boundary arc; isolated discontinuities are admissible, and further regularity is assumed only for convenience.
results.modern_name: Dirichlet problem with piecewise-continuous boundary data / finite-energy (H^1) admissibility; point singularities have zero capacity
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1851 dissertation; 1857 Abelian functions), building on Green, Gauss, Dirichlet; rigor by Hilbert (1900)

results.what: A dependence law is 'simpler' the fewer quantity operations (± , ×, ÷, differentiation, integration) are needed to determine it; these operations are those for which commensurability is irrelevant.
results.modern_name: Informal complexity of closed-form expressions / programmatic definition of 'analytic expression' (cf. Art. 20 of the dissertation)

deep.surprise_reason: Both passages are draft wordings of statements that appear (nearly verbatim, as I recall) in Riemann's published 1851 dissertation. They contain no new mathematics.
transcription_corrections: Line 4: before 'weitere' there is a struck or overwritten word that is not legible ('[-...-]'). The sense, and the published wording as I recall it, suggest it should read as a new sentence: 'die weitere Beschränkung ist nur gemacht...'.

Line 5: 'unnöthige' is visibly struck through or overwritten in the image, consistent with the given '[-unnöthige-]'. However, the printed dissertation (as I recall it) retains 'unnöthige Weitläufigkeiten'.
There is a stray opening parenthesis '(' at the end of line 5 in the manuscript, after 'vermeiden'; the transcription omits it.
'einfacher' and 'indem' are underlined in the manuscript. 'indem' is struck, and 'bedingt wird, wir' is inserted above the line, as transcribed.
'Theile' is underlined in line 3; 'Weitläufigkeiten' is underlined in line 5.
